title: Patient Communication and Positioning Assistance

unit.title: Clinical Office Practice and Patient Safety

sections.learningObjectives:
- Communicate with patients respectfully using plain language, active listening, and appropriate nonverbal cues.
- Assist with patient positioning only as directed by the licensed clinician and within the assistant's training.
- Maintain patient comfort, dignity, and safety using proper body mechanics, draping, and infection control.
- Recognize the limits of the assistant's scope of practice and escalate appropriately.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Imagine being scared at a doctor visit and someone talks to you kindly and really listens. That kind, listening talk helps you feel safe, which is exactly what therapeutic communication does.

### Question 2

When you meet someone new at school you say your name first. In a medical office the assistant does the same so the patient knows exactly who is helping them.

### Question 3

If a friend explains a game using words you already know, you understand it better. Plain language does the same thing for medical information.

### Question 4

Active listening is like really paying attention to a friend telling a story and then repeating the important part back so they know you got it.

### Question 5

A yes-or-no question is like a door that only opens a crack. An open-ended question swings the door wide open so the patient can tell you the whole story.

### Question 6

Teach-back is like repeating the directions back to someone who gave them, to make sure you both agree on where to go.

### Question 7

Everyone likes to be called the name they choose, just like you might prefer a nickname over your full name. Using it shows you respect them.

### Question 8

When a friend turns toward you and looks at you while you talk, you know they care. Facing a patient and making eye contact shows the same thing.

### Question 9

Some things are private, like a secret you only tell one friend. Health details are private too, so the assistant keeps them where only the patient can hear.

### Question 10

You would want to know before someone moves your chair, right? The assistant tells the patient what they will do first so there are no surprises.

### Question 11

When a friend is scared, you say you understand instead of telling them to just stop worrying. The assistant does the same for a worried patient.

### Question 12

Only the person with the special training can explain what a tricky test score means. The assistant points the patient to the right person instead of guessing.

### Question 13

It is easier to understand someone when you can see their face and the room is quiet. The assistant makes it easier by doing both.

### Question 14

Just because someone uses a wheelchair does not mean they need help with everything. The assistant asks first, the same way you would ask a friend what they need.

### Question 15

Different families have different customs about personal space. Asking politely what someone is comfortable with is the kind and safe thing to do.

### Question 16

When someone is upset, staying calm is like being the still person in the room; it helps the other person settle down instead of getting louder.

### Question 17

You would not like being cut off mid-sentence. The assistant waits and listens until the patient is finished talking.

### Question 18

Writing down exactly what someone said is like taking careful notes so nothing important gets lost or changed.

### Question 19

Only the doctor has the training to say what might happen next. The assistant helps by sending the question to the person who can answer it.

### Question 20

Sitting at the same height as someone makes talking feel friendly and equal, like sitting at a table with a friend.

### Question 21

If you do not understand something, it is better to ask than to guess. The assistant politely asks the patient to say it again.

### Question 22

Repeating directions out loud is like checking a list before you leave the house, so nothing important is forgotten.

### Question 23

A patient's health details are like a private secret that should only be shared where no one else can hear.

### Question 24

If a friend looks confused while you explain a game, you stop and check in. The assistant does the same when a patient looks puzzled.

### Question 25

Special words only some people know can feel like a secret code. Plain words make sure everyone understands the same thing.

### Question 26

Choosing medicine is a job for the trained person, like how only a mechanic should choose a part for your bike. The assistant sends the question to the right person.

### Question 27

It is easier to tell a secret to someone who will not make fun of you. The assistant listens kindly so the patient feels safe to share.

### Question 28

Sometimes a quiet pause lets a person find the right words, like taking a breath before answering a hard question.

### Question 29

The person leading the check-up decides how the patient should sit or lie, and the assistant helps them get there safely.

### Question 30

The Fowler position is like sitting up in a recliner, with the top of the table lifted so the patient is almost upright.

### Question 31

Supine is like lying on your back looking up at the ceiling.

### Question 32

Prone is like lying on your tummy, the way you might lie to have someone look at your back.

### Question 33

The Sims position is like lying on your side with one leg straight and the other pulled up, like a side-sleeping position.

### Question 34

The lithotomy position is like lying on your back with your knees up and legs resting on little supports, so the clinician can do a pelvic check.

### Question 35

Trendelenburg is like tipping a board so your feet are up and your head is down.

### Question 36

Dorsal recumbent is like lying on your back with your knees up and your feet resting on the table.

### Question 37

The knee-chest position is like kneeling and leaning all the way forward so your chest touches the table.

### Question 38

To look at your tummy, the clinician needs you lying on your back, like the supine position.

### Question 39

For a rectal check, the patient lies on their side with one leg bent up, like the Sims position, so the clinician can see what they need to.

### Question 40

To look at your back, you either stand up or lie on your tummy so the clinician can see it clearly.

### Question 41

To look in your ear, the clinician needs you sitting up so your head is at a good height to see into.

### Question 42

It is easier to climb onto a low seat than a high one. The assistant lowers the table and adds a step so the patient can get up safely.

### Question 43

A gait belt is like a strong strap around the patient's middle that the assistant holds, so the patient has extra support while moving.

### Question 44

When you pick up a heavy backpack, you bend your knees and keep your back straight so your legs do the work instead of hurting your back.

### Question 45

When a box is too heavy for one person, you get a friend to help. The assistant does the same when a patient needs more than one person to move safely.

### Question 46

You lock a bike before you step away, and the assistant locks the wheelchair wheels before the patient gets out, so it stays still.

### Question 47

If a friend is wobbly on a tall chair, you stay close in case they slip. The assistant stays close to a wobbly patient too.

### Question 48

If a patient has a tube attached, you move gently around it so it does not get yanked out, like being careful near a delicate string.

### Question 49

A drape is like a cozy blanket that keeps the patient covered and comfortable while the clinician does the check-up.

### Question 50

You would want someone to ask before they moved your leg. The assistant asks first and explains, so the patient knows what is happening.

### Question 51

If a friend feels faint, you sit them down and get help right away. The assistant does the same and tells the clinician.

### Question 52

When you sit up fast you can feel dizzy. Waiting a moment before standing helps the patient feel steady first.

### Question 53

A tidy room with nothing on the floor is like a clear path to the door; there is nothing to trip over.

### Question 54

When you are cold, a blanket feels nice. The assistant offers one so the patient is cozy and comfortable.

### Question 55

Before leaving, the assistant makes sure the patient knows how to push the help button, like knowing how to ring a doorbell.

### Question 56

Sitting on a hard chair too long gets uncomfortable. Adding a soft cushion and checking in keeps the patient comfortable during a long exam.

### Question 57

When you lower a baby into a crib, you support their head. The assistant supports the patient's head and body the same way when lying them back.

### Question 58

If you are not sure how to do something, it is safer to say so and ask for help than to guess and risk a mistake.

### Question 59

Washing hands before and after helping someone is like washing your hands before and after eating, so germs do not travel either way.

### Question 60

Treating everyone with the same careful steps is like always wearing a seatbelt, even for short rides, just in case.

### Question 61

Gloves are like dish gloves that protect your hands from messy things, so the assistant wears them before touching anything wet like blood.

### Question 62

After taking off messy gloves, you still wash your hands, because some mess can sneak onto them when the gloves come off.

### Question 63

You wipe a table between people using it, just like you wipe a lunch table before the next person sits down.

### Question 64

Treating every drop of blood like it could carry germs is like treating every raw egg as if it could be cracked, just to be safe.

### Question 65

A used needle goes straight into a special strong box, like throwing a sharp pencil into a sturdy bin instead of leaving it on the desk.

### Question 66

If you spill something messy on your skin, you wash it off right away with soap and water. The assistant does the same after touching blood.

### Question 67

Covering a cough is like catching sneezes in your elbow so the germs stay with you instead of flying to friends.

### Question 68

You wear rain boots only when it is rainy, not on a sunny day. The assistant picks protection based on what might splash or touch them during the task.

### Question 69

Carrying a messy cloth away from your clothes and not waving it around keeps the mess from getting on you or in the air.

### Question 70

Clean hands are the number one secret to not sharing germs, like washing hands before sharing snacks.

### Question 71

When your hands are really muddy, you need soap and water to get the mud off; a quick wipe is not enough.

### Question 72

If your gloves are dirty, you do not touch your face or your phone with them, or the dirt spreads everywhere.

### Question 73

When the sharp box is full, you get a new box instead of stuffing it, so nothing sharp pokes out and hurts someone.

### Question 74

If you get a door knob messy, you clean the knob and wash your hands so the mess does not spread to other things.

### Question 75

If something unsafe happens at work, you tell the right person right away so they can help, not wait for weeks.

### Question 76

If you see something unusual, you tell the grown-up in charge instead of guessing what it is. The assistant tells the clinician.

### Question 77

Only the person with the right training can name what a skin spot is. The assistant points the patient to the clinician instead of guessing.

### Question 78

If you are not sure what a coach wants you to do, you ask instead of guessing, so you do the right thing the first time.

### Question 79

Giving medicine is a job only for specially trained people. The assistant says no and asks the right person to do it.

### Question 80

If a plan seems unsafe, it is okay to speak up and ask, 'Are you sure?' so everyone stays safe.

### Question 81

If someone suddenly has trouble breathing, you get help right away instead of waiting to see what happens.

### Question 82

Writing down what happened right away is like jotting a note so you remember exactly what you did and how it went.

### Question 83

If the first grown-up cannot help, you tell the next grown-up in charge so the problem still gets fixed.

### Question 84

The assistant helps move a patient only when the person in charge says so and the assistant knows how to do it safely.

### Question 85

Knowing which jobs are yours and which are not is like knowing not to touch a hot stove; it keeps everyone safe and out of trouble.
